{{Short description|Operation on pairs of integer sequences}}

'''Dyson's transform''' is a fundamental technique in [[additive number theory]] for transforming a pair of [[integer sequence]]s into another pair of integer sequences.<ref name="nathanson">{{Cite book |last=Nathanson |first=Melvyn B. |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=PqlQjNhjkKUC&q=%22e-transform%22 |title=Additive Number Theory: Inverse Problems and the Geometry of Sumsets |date=1996-08-22 |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |isbn=978-0-387-94655-9 |language=en}}</ref> It was developed by [[Freeman Dyson]] as part of his proof of [[Mann's theorem]] on the [[Schnirelmann density]] of [[sumset]]s,<ref name="Sequences">{{cite book | last1 = Halberstam | first1 = H. |authorlink1 = Heini Halberstam | last2 = Roth | first2 = K. F. | authorlink2 =Klaus Roth | title = Sequences | title-link=Sequences (book) | publisher = Springer-Verlag | location = Berlin | year = 1983 | edition = revised | isbn = 978-0-387-90801-4 }}</ref>{{Rp|17}} is used to prove such fundamental results of additive number theory as the [[Cauchy–Davenport theorem]] on the size of [[restricted sumset]]s,<ref name=nathanson /> and was used by [[Olivier Ramaré]] in his work (related to the [[Goldbach conjecture]]) that proved that every even integer is the sum of at most 6 [[prime number]]s.<ref name="Ramaré">{{cite journal | author=O. Ramaré | authorlink=Olivier Ramaré | title=On šnirel'man's constant | journal=Annali della Scuola Normale Superiore di Pisa. Classe di Scienze. Serie IV | volume=22 | year=1995 | issue=4 | pages=645–706 | url = http://www.numdam.org/item?id=ASNSP_1995_4_22_4_645_0 | accessdate = 2009-03-13}}</ref>{{Rp|700–701}} The term ''Dyson's transform'' for this technique is used by Ramaré.<ref name="Ramaré" />{{Rp|700–701}} Halberstam and Roth call it the τ-transformation.<ref name="Sequences"/>{{Rp|58}}

==Formulation==
This formulation of the transform is from Ramaré.<ref name="Ramaré" />{{Rp|700–701}} Let <math>A</math> be a sequence of natural numbers, and <math>x</math> be any [[real number]]. Write <math>A(x)</math> for the number of elements of <math>A</math> which lie in <math>[1,x]</math>. Suppose <math>A= \{a_1<a_2< \cdots\}</math> and <math>B= \{0=b_1<b_2<\cdots\} </math> are two sequences of natural numbers. We write <math>A+B</math> for the [[sumset]], that is, the set of all elements <math>a+b</math> where <math>a</math> is in <math>A</math> and <math>b</math> is in <math>B</math>; and similarly <math>A-B</math> for the set of differences <math>a-b</math>. For any element <math>e</math> in <math>A</math>, Dyson's transform consists in forming the sequences <math> A'= A \cup (B + \{e\})</math>  and  <math>\,B'= B \cap (A - \{e\})</math>.

==Properties==
The transformed sequences have the properties:

* <math>A' + B' \subset A + B </math>
* <math>\{e\} + B' \subset A' </math>
* <math>0 \in B' </math>
* <math>A'(m)+ B'(m-e) = A(m) + B(m-e) </math>

==Related transforms==
Other closely related transforms are sometimes referred to as Dyson transforms. This includes the transform defined by <math>A_1 = A \cap (A + \{e\})</math>, <math>A_2 = A \cup (A + \{e\})</math>, <math>B_1 = B \cap (-\{e\} + B)</math>, <math>B_2 = B \cup (-\{e\} + B)</math> for <math>A, B</math> sets in a (not necessarily abelian) group. This transformation has the property that   

* <math>A_1 + B_1 \subset A + B, A_2 + B_2 \subset A + B </math>
* <math>|A_1| + |A_2| = 2|A| </math>, <math>|B_1| + |B_2| = 2|B| </math>
It can be used to prove a generalisation of the [[Cauchy-Davenport theorem]].<ref>{{Cite journal |last=DeVos |first=Matt |date=2016 |title=On a Generalization of the Cauchy-Davenport Theorem |url=http://math.colgate.edu/~integers/q7/q7.Abstract.html |journal=Integers |volume=16}}</ref>
